summary.text: 重 is used for “heavy” and “double; repeated.” A Han-dynasty dictionary analyzes 壬 as semantic and 東 as phonetic, glossing the character “thick/deep.” A separate proposal pictures a person carrying a load; another interprets 東 as a sack and 土 beneath it as a weight. The graph’s origin remains unsettled.

formation.text: The Han-dynasty dictionary gives a phonosemantic analysis: 壬 contributes meaning and 東 supplies sound, alongside the whole-character gloss “thick/deep.” Distinct proposals picture a person carrying a load, or identify 東 as a sack with 土 beneath it as a weight. The original construction is unresolved; the sack proposal does not establish that 土 was added later.

components.text: The Han-dynasty dictionary identifies 壬 as the semantic element in 重. Its gloss for the whole character is “thick/deep”; this analysis does not establish the graph’s original referent.
The Han-dynasty dictionary assigns 東 a phonetic role. The available reading comparison is modern and does not independently prove that role or an ancient sound relationship.

sound_limitation.text: The modern Mandarin pair does not establish 東 as the phonetic element in this graph or prove an ancient sound relationship.

sound.text: The current Mandarin readings differ; this pair does not demonstrate the historical analysis.

history.text: A bronze-script-style redraw shows a tall, bulbous form on the left and a branching form with several openings on the right. It is not tied to a dated inscription, so it cannot establish an early form or a sequence of graphic changes.

The transmitted Han-dynasty dictionary analyzes 重 as 壬 semantic plus 東 phonetic. Another proposal pictures a person carrying a load; a distinct account interprets 東 as a sack and 土 beneath it as a weight. Neither the original referent nor a later addition of 土 is established.

An index lists Qin and Han materials, but no dated, contextual inscription was identified. The earliest secure graphic attestation remains unresolved. No object name or pronunciation is established for a proposed borrowing from a pictured load or sack.

uncertainties.text: The dictionary’s 壬-plus-東 analysis, the person-carrying-load account, and the sack-and-weight proposal are distinct explanations; the evidence does not determine which explains the graph’s origin.
The original name or pronunciation of the proposed load or sack is not established, so borrowing the graph from such an object’s name is unsupported.
The timing and development of “thick/deep,” “heavy,” “weight,” “solemn/respectful,” and “repeat/overlap” are unresolved. The proposed relationship between 重 and 緟 is also unverified.

“Heavy” is a documented current meaning; its emergence relative to the dictionary gloss “thick; deep” is undated.
“Double” is a documented current meaning, and historical phonology data associate a reading with “repeat; double.” The evidence does not date this sense or show that it developed from “thick; deep.”
Historical phonology data record a noun meaning “weight”; its chronology relative to “heavy” is unresolved.
A historical commentary proposes this sense as an extension of “thick; deep,” but its timing is not established.

developments.text: A historical commentary links “solemn; respectful” to “thick; deep”; dated evidence for this development is unavailable.

limitations.text: The earliest dated use of the listed meanings is not identified. Dictionary glosses and reading metadata do not establish a chronology.
The proposal that 重 replaced 緟 for “overlap; repeat” is disputed and does not establish a semantic or graphic development.

evidence.text: 厚也。从壬東聲。凡重之屬皆从重。

evidence.source: wiktionary
evidence.text:
Phono-semantic compound (形聲 /形声, OC *doŋ, *doŋʔ, *doŋs) and ideogrammic compound (會意 /会意): semantic 人 (“man”) + phonetic 東 (OC *toːŋ, “bag”) – a man carrying a bag. A glyph 土 (“earth”) was later added to show that the bag-carrying man is standing on the ground. From this composition (𡍺) is the current form. In the modern form, the man on top can be seen as 亻 (however, the upper part of the character is unrelated to 千).
See also 以, in which a person is carrying something, 央, in which a person is carrying a pole, and 年, in which a person is carrying the harvest.
Schuessler (2007) notes that the etymology is uncertain and compares the word to Burmese စုံ (cum, “to be sufficient; pair”), which STEDT puts under Proto-Sino-Tibetan *dzum ~ tsum (“pair”).
Pronunciation 3 is the exoactive derivation of pronunciation 1.

evidence.source: Shuowen Jiezi, online text and Duan Yucai commentary
evidence.text: The Han-dynasty dictionary defines 重 as “thick/deep” (厚), analyzes it as 从壬東聲 (“壬 as semantic element, 東 as phonetic”), and treats characters in its series as written with 重. Duan Yucai says the senses “solemn/respectful” and “repeated/overlapping” are extensions from 厚, and comments that ancient usage had only the level-tone reading, without the departing-tone reading. This is a historical analysis, not independent confirmation of the graph's origin.
evidence.title: 說文解字「重」 - Shuowen.org

evidence.source: Kotobank, Japanese dictionary entry citing Shuowen and later lexicographic tradition
evidence.text: The entry records competing analyses: its own graphic account treats 東 as an image of a sack and 土 beneath it as a weight, while its account of the Shuowen analysis gives 壬 as semantic and 東 as phonetic. It lists senses including heavy, overlap/add, weighty or deep, solemn/respectable, slow/careful, worry, pregnancy, and swelling. These are dictionary-listed senses, not a dated semantic chronology; the sack-and-weight interpretation is not independently established by this source.
evidence.title: 重(ジュウ)とは？ 意味・読み方 - コトバンク

evidence.source: Wiktionary, Chinese entry; historical-form links and cited phonological source labels
evidence.field: graphic history, phonetic series, competing account
evidence.text: The page presents period-labeled glyph images for Shang, Western Zhou, Warring States, and the Shuowen small-seal tradition, but the page text alone does not establish each image's provenance or provide an inscription citation. It proposes a 人 + 東 account, with 東 as phonetic and a later 土 element, while noting Schuessler's caution that the word etymology is uncertain. It separately lists 重 in a Zhengzhang (2003) phonetic series at *doŋ, *doŋʔ, *doŋs, and lists 緟 at *doŋ, *doŋs. Its proposal that “overlap” first belonged to 緟 and was later replaced by 重 is not established here with dated attestations; treat it as a disputed lexical account, distinct from the graph's proposed 東 sound component.
evidence.title: 重 - Wiktionary

evidence.source: Shuowen Jiezi, online text and Duan Yucai commentary
evidence.text: The Han-dynasty dictionary defines 重 as “thick/deep” (厚), analyzes it as 从壬東聲 (“壬 as semantic element, 東 as phonetic”), and treats characters in its series as written with 重. Duan Yucai says the senses “solemn/respectful” and “repeated/overlapping” are extensions from 厚, and comments that ancient usage had only the level-tone reading, without the departing-tone reading. This is a historical analysis, not independent confirmation of the graph's origin.
evidence.title: 說文解字「重」 - Shuowen.org

evidence.source: Kotobank, Japanese dictionary entry citing Shuowen and later lexicographic tradition
evidence.text: The entry records competing analyses: its own graphic account treats 東 as an image of a sack and 土 beneath it as a weight, while its account of the Shuowen analysis gives 壬 as semantic and 東 as phonetic. It lists senses including heavy, overlap/add, weighty or deep, solemn/respectable, slow/careful, worry, pregnancy, and swelling. These are dictionary-listed senses, not a dated semantic chronology; the sack-and-weight interpretation is not independently established by this source.
evidence.title: 重(ジュウ)とは？ 意味・読み方 - コトバンク

evidence.source: Wiktionary, Chinese entry; historical-form links and cited phonological source labels
evidence.field: graphic history, phonetic series, competing account
evidence.text: The page presents period-labeled glyph images for Shang, Western Zhou, Warring States, and the Shuowen small-seal tradition, but the page text alone does not establish each image's provenance or provide an inscription citation. It proposes a 人 + 東 account, with 東 as phonetic and a later 土 element, while noting Schuessler's caution that the word etymology is uncertain. It separately lists 重 in a Zhengzhang (2003) phonetic series at *doŋ, *doŋʔ, *doŋs, and lists 緟 at *doŋ, *doŋs. Its proposal that “overlap” first belonged to 緟 and was later replaced by 重 is not established here with dated attestations; treat it as a disputed lexical account, distinct from the graph's proposed 東 sound component.
evidence.title: 重 - Wiktionary

editorial_rules: Write about the character's graphic history; distinguish it from the history of a spoken word.
Separate historical explanation from mnemonics. Do not infer history from modern shapes or readings.
Sources may repeat one another. A source count is not independent corroboration.
Treat Shuowen as a historical account, not automatic confirmation. Its generated English glosses are excluded.
Unrelated word senses may appear in Wiktionary excerpts. Do not merge them into a character origin.
Related-character evidence retains its record_character. Do not silently transfer a traditional form's components to a simplified form.
No glyph image has been visually inspected in this packet. Do not claim to have inspected one.
Explain missing evidence explicitly, especially for Japanese-created characters. A Chinese spelling pronunciation is not evidence for a Japanese origin.

gaps: No specific primary oracle-bone or bronze inscription containing 重 was retrieved and read in context. Earliest secure graphic attestation, inscription date, and earliest attested word-sense therefore remain unresolved here.

Shuowen's 壬/東 analysis, a person-carrying-load analysis, and the sack/earth-weight proposal conflict. Accessible sources do not establish whether 東 originally depicted a bag, nor do they prove 土 was added later as a ground marker. No original object name/pronunciation was independently established, so no sound-based borrowing from a bag name is demonstrated.

The lexical development from “thick/deep” to “heavy,” “weight,” “solemn/respectful,” and “repeat/overlap” lacks dated contextual attestations in the inspected primary material. Dictionary gloss order is not chronology.

The claim that 重 replaced 緟 for “overlap/repeat” is a separate disputed word-history proposal. No dated textual witnesses or phonological argument sufficient to establish the replacement were inspected.

A current Mandarin reading for 東 and its exact Baxter–Sagart row were not verified. The local 重 row is preserved as provided; it does not independently demonstrate 東's phonetic role. The official Unihan endpoints for both characters failed to open.

No reproducible versioned extract recommendation: cited pages provide character-specific dictionary/paleographic information, and no clearly applicable bulk-reuse permission for such an extract was verified.
No primary oracle-bone or bronze token for 重 was retrieved with an inscription identifier, date, and contextual reading; earliest secure graphic attestation remains unresolved.

The source page for the Commons Shang-style oracle redraw does not identify an inscription or validate that the graph was actually used in Shang-period records. Treat it only as a sourced image candidate, not evidence for an early date or meaning.

The accounts involving a person carrying a load, 東 as a sack, and 土 as added ground remain disputed; the original referent and any name/pronunciation for a depicted object are not securely established. A source-word/object-name borrowing claim is therefore unsupported.

The lexical histories of “thick/deep,” “heavy,” “weight,” “solemn/respectful,” and “repeat/overlap” remain undated in the inspected primary material. The proposed 重/緟 replacement is likewise unresolved.
The exact Unicode character pages for 重 and 東 could not be opened. Local rows were available and preserved, but official character-specific Unihan click-through evidence is unavailable.
No versioned extract is recommended: no applicable bulk-reuse permission was established and the useful sources are character-specific.

No primary inscription containing 重 with an inscription identifier, date, and contextual reading was retrieved. The earliest secure graphic attestation and earliest dated word senses remain unresolved.

The Shuowen 壬 + 東 analysis is documented as a Han-dynasty dictionary account. Competing person-carrying-load and 東-as-bag interpretations are present in the dossier, but this search did not independently establish the original referent or show that 土 was added later. No depicted object’s name and pronunciation were established for a sound-based whole-graph borrowing claim.

No dated contextual attestations were found to establish when the senses “thick/deep,” “heavy,” “weight,” “solemn/respectful,” or “repeat/overlap” arose. Dictionary gloss order is not chronology. The proposed 重/緟 replacement remains unresolved.
